title: DATA STRUCTURES, GRAPHS & HASHING
description: Interactive Revision Cheat Sheet & Interview Guide covering linear and non-linear data structures, graphs, hashing, patterns, interview Q&A, and memory maps.

sections.title: Data Structures Overview
sections.description: Foundational introduction to data structures and their primary categories.

topics.title: DATA STRUCTURES OVERVIEW
topics.explanation:
-Data Structure: Data structure is a way of organizing and storing data so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently. The main categories are:
->Linear Data Structures : Elements are arranged sequentially. Examples: Arrays, Strings, Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues. 
->Non-Linear Data Structures : Elements are organized hierarchically or as networks. Examples: Trees, Heaps, Graphs, Hash Tables
topics.tldr: Data Structure হলো data এমনভাবে organize করা যাতে efficiently use করা যায়।

questions.question: Is a Hash Table linear or non-linear?
questions.answer: It is usually categorized separately as a hash-based data structure. Unlike arrays or linked lists, it uses a hash function to determine where data is stored.

traps.statement: Is a Hash Table linear or non-linear?
traps.explanation: It is usually categorized separately as a hash-based data structure. Unlike arrays or linked lists, it uses a hash function to determine where data is stored.

sections.title: PART 1: LINEAR DATA STRUCTURES
sections.description: Sequential memory and node-based linear data structures.

topics.title: ARRAYS
topics.explanation: -Array: An array is a collection of elements stored in contiguous memory locations. Because elements are stored continuously, an element can be accessed directly using its index.
topics.tldr: Array index দিয়ে খুব fast access দেয়, কিন্তু মাঝখানে insert/delete করতে shifting লাগে।
keyPoints: Insertions and deletions may require shifting
Searching for an arbitrary value is O(n)

codeSnippets.explanation: C++ Array Operations traversal, insertion with shift, and deletion with shift.

questions.question: Is array searching always O(1)?
questions.answer: No. Accessing by index is O(1), but searching for a value using linear search is O(n).

traps.statement: Array lookup and array search are both O(1).
traps.explanation: Access by index is O(1). Searching for a value is usually O(n).

topics.title: STRINGS
topics.explanation:
-String: String is a sequence/array of characters.
Essential Operations:Length, Character Access, Uppercase, Lowercase, Find, Search, Contains, Substring, Replace, Split, Join, Trim, Concatenate, Compare, Repeat.
Important Note: Strings are immutable in many languages (e.g., JavaScript, Python). This means that once a string is created, its characters cannot be changed directly. Instead, operations that modify a string typically create a new string.
topics.tldr: JavaScript string-এর character direct change করা যায় না কারণ String immutable।

codeSnippets.explanation: Demonstration of string immutability in JavaScript.

questions.question: Does immutability mean a variable cannot be reassigned?
questions.answer: No. The string value is immutable, but a variable can be reassigned to a new string.

comparisons.title: Common String Operations
rows: Returns -1, false, or an error if the item is missing

traps.statement: Does immutability mean a variable cannot be reassigned?
traps.explanation: No. The string value is immutable, but a variable can be reassigned to a new string.

topics.title: DYNAMIC ARRAYS — C++ VECTOR
topics.explanation:
-Vector: Vector is a dynamic array in C++. Unlike a traditional fixed-size array, a vector can grow automatically.
If a vector runs out of capacity: A larger memory block is allocated. Existing elements are moved or copied. The old memory is released. The vector continues using the new block.
topics.tldr: vector::push_back() সাধারণত O(1), তবে resize হলে existing elements copy/move করতে O(n) লাগে।

questions.question: Is every push_back() operation strictly O(1)?
questions.answer: No. It is amortized O(1). A resize operation may require moving O(n) elements.

traps.statement: Every vector push_back() is O(1).
traps.explanation: It is amortized O(1). Resizing can take O(n).

topics.title: LINKED LISTS
topics.explanation:
-Linked List: A linked list is a linear data structure where elements are stored in nodes. Each node contains data and a pointer/reference to another node.
Comparison: Unlike arrays, nodes do not need to be stored contiguously in memory.
->Singly Linked List: Each node points to the next node.
->Doubly Linked List: Each node contains pointers to both next and previous nodes, allowing traversal in both directions at the cost of additional pointer memory.

 Important Note: In C++, struct and class are identical in capability; the only default difference is that struct members are public by default, whereas class members are private.
topics.tldr: Array fast indexing দেয়, Linked List fast insertion/deletion দিতে পারে যদি node আগে থেকেই জানা থাকে।

codeSnippets.explanation: C++ Singly Linked List insertion and deletion implementations.

questions.question: Is insertion in a linked list always O(1)?
questions.answer: No. It is O(1) only when the insertion position or node reference is already known. Finding the position may take O(n).

traps.statement: Linked List insertion is always O(1).
traps.explanation: It is O(1) only when the insertion position is already known.

topics.title: STACK
topics.explanation:
-Stack: Stack is a linear data structure that strictly follows the Last In, First Out (LIFO) principle—the last element inserted is the first one to be removed.

Core Operations: Push (insert onto top), Pop (remove from top), and Top/Peek (inspect top element), all running in O(1) time.
Common Applications: Function call stacks & recursion, undo/redo mechanisms, balanced parentheses parsing, arithmetic expression evaluation, browser history navigation, and Depth-First Search (DFS).
topics.tldr: Stack-এ যেটা সবশেষে ঢোকে, সেটাই আগে বের হয়।
examples:
Input: hello
Stack: h e l l o
Output: olleh

questions.question: What happens if you call pop() on an empty stack?
questions.answer: It is invalid. Always check whether the stack is empty before accessing or removing elements.

traps.statement: What happens if you call pop() on an empty stack?
traps.explanation: It is invalid. Always check whether the stack is empty before accessing or removing elements.

topics.title: QUEUE
topics.explanation:
-Queue: A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First In, First Out (FIFO) principle—the first element added is the first one to be processed.

Core Operations: Enqueue (insert at rear), Dequeue (remove from front), and Front/Peek (inspect front element), all operating in O(1) time.
Common Applications: CPU task scheduling, print spoolers, asynchronous message buffering, request handling pipelines, Breadth-First Search (BFS), and producer-consumer architectures.
topics.tldr: Queue-তে যেটা প্রথমে ঢোকে, সেটাই সবার আগে বের হয় (FIFO)।
examples:
Enqueue: 10 -> 20 -> 30
Queue State: [Front: 10, 20, 30: Rear]
Dequeue: 10 (Front moves to 20)

codeSnippets.explanation: C++ Queue standard operations: push (enqueue), pop (dequeue), and front inspection.

topics.title: CIRCULAR QUEUE
topics.explanation: -Circular Queue: Circular queue is a linear data structure where the last position is connected back to the first position to form a ring.
topics.tldr: Queue-এর শেষ index থেকে আবার শুরুতে ফিরে আসলে সেটাই Circular Queue।

questions.question: Why use a circular queue?
questions.answer: It efficiently reuses empty spaces created after dequeue operations.

traps.statement: Why use a circular queue?
traps.explanation: It efficiently reuses empty spaces created after dequeue operations.

topics.title: STACK VS QUEUE
topics.explanation:
Stack (LIFO) and Queue (FIFO) are fundamental linear structures with contrasting access models.
Difference:Stacks restrict insertion and deletion to a single end (Top), whereas Queues enforce two-ended access (Enqueue at Rear, Dequeue from Front).

comparisons.title: Stack vs Queue
rows: Add at rear, remove from front

sections.title: PART 2: NON-LINEAR DATA STRUCTURES
sections.description: Hierarchical, priority, and network data structures.

topics.title: TREES
topics.explanation:
Tree: A tree is a non-linear hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes connected by directed or undirected edges, forming an acyclic structure.
Key Terminology: Includes Root (uppermost node), Parent/Child (hierarchical connections), Leaves (nodes with zero children), Subtrees, Depth (distance from root), and Height (longest path to a leaf).
topics.tldr: Tree হলো parent-child relationship দিয়ে তৈরি hierarchical structure।

questions.question: Can a tree contain cycles?
questions.answer: A standard tree does not contain cycles.

traps.statement: Can a tree contain cycles?
traps.explanation: A standard tree does not contain cycles.

topics.title: BINARY TREE
topics.explanation: -Binary Tree: A binary tree is a hierarchical tree data structure in which every node has at most two children, referred to as the left child and the right child.

topics.title: 12. BINARY SEARCH TREE (BST)
topics.explanation: -Binary Search Tree: A Binary Search Tree (BST) stores smaller values in the left subtree and larger values in the right subtree. This enables fast O(log n) average search, insert, and delete.
topics.tldr: BST-তে ছোট value left, বড় value right। Balanced হলে fast, skewed হলে slow।

questions.question: Is BST search always O(log n)?
questions.answer: No. In a skewed BST, search can degrade to O(n).

traps.statement: BST operations are always O(log n).
traps.explanation: A skewed BST can degrade to O(n).

topics.title: TREE TRAVERSALS
topics.explanation:
Tree traversal algorithms systematically visit every node in O(n) time.

- Depth-First Traversal (DFS): Explores a tree by going as deep as possible before going back.
 The three main types are: 
Inorder(Left → Root → Right): Yields values in sorted ascending order for valid BSTs.
Preorder(Root → Left → Right): Commonly used for copying, serialization, and prefix expression trees.
Postorder(Left → Right → Root): Processes descendants before ancestors, ideal for deletion and postfix tree evaluations.

- Breadth-First Traversal: Explores the tree level by level using an explicit FIFO Queue.
topics.tldr: Inorder BST sorted দেয়, Preorder root আগে, Postorder root শেষে, Level Order level ধরে চলে।

questions.question: Does inorder traversal always produce sorted output?
questions.answer: No. It produces sorted output only when the tree is a valid BST.

traps.statement: Inorder traversal always returns sorted values.
traps.explanation: Only for a valid Binary Search Tree.

topics.title: HEAPS
topics.explanation:
-Heap: A heap is a specialized complete binary tree that satisfies the heap property.
Max Heap: every parent node is greater than or equal to its children, placing the maximum element at the root.
Min Heap: every parent node is less than or equal to its children, placing the minimum element at the root.

topics.title: 15. PRIORITY QUEUE
topics.explanation: -Priority Queue: A priority queue is an abstract data type where each element has an assigned priority, ensuring that higher-priority elements are dequeued before lower-priority ones, regardless of arrival order.
topics.tldr: Heap সব data sort করে রাখে না—শুধু top priority element efficiently রাখে।

questions.question: Is a heap fully sorted?
questions.answer: No. Only the parent-child heap property is guaranteed.

traps.statement: A Heap is fully sorted.
traps.explanation: A Heap only guarantees parent-child ordering.

topics.title: GRAPHS
topics.explanation:
-Graph: A graph G = (V, E) is a non-linear data structure comprising a set of vertices (nodes) and edges (connections between vertices). Graphs can be directed (edges have fixed one-way direction) or undirected (bidirectional edges), as well as weighted (edges carry numerical costs) or unweighted.
Difference: Unlike trees, graphs can contain cycles, self-loops, and multiple disconnected components.

topics.title: 17. ADJACENCY MATRIX
topics.explanation:
-Adjacency Matrix: An adjacency matrix represents a graph using a 2D array of size V × V, where cell matrix[u][v] indicates the presence (or weight) of an edge between vertices u and v.
Optimal: It is best suited for dense graphs.
topics.tldr: Matrix edge আছে কিনা fast check করে, কিন্তু অনেক memory নেয়।

questions.question: Is an adjacency matrix good for sparse graphs?
questions.answer: Usually no, because it still uses O(V²) memory even when there are few edges.

traps.statement: Is an adjacency matrix good for sparse graphs?
traps.explanation: Usually no, because it still uses O(V²) memory even when there are few edges.

topics.title: ADJACENCY LIST
topics.explanation:
-Adjacency List: An adjacency list represents a graph as an array or vector of collections, where index u stores a dynamic list of all immediate neighbors adjacent to vertex u. By allocating memory proportional only to existing edges, it achieves optimal O(V + E) space efficiency.
 Optimal: It is ideal for sparse graphs.

topics.title: ADJACENCY MATRIX VS ADJACENCY LIST
topics.explanation: Difference:Adjacency Matrix offers O(1) edge checks but wastes O(V²) space, making it ideal for dense graphs. Adjacency List uses O(V + E) space and iterates neighbors faster, but edge lookups take O(degree) time, making it ideal for sparse graphs.
topics.tldr: Dense graph হলে Matrix, Sparse graph হলে List বেশি ভালো।

questions.question: Which representation is generally preferred for sparse graphs?
questions.answer: Adjacency List because it uses O(V + E) space.

topics.title: GRAPH VISITED ARRAY
topics.explanation: ->Graphs can have cycles, so a visited tracker (array or set) is required to prevent infinite loops and re-processing nodes. For disconnected graphs, loop through all vertices to start traversals from every unvisited component.
topics.tldr: Graph-এ cycle থাকতে পারে, তাই একই node বারবার না যেতে visited লাগে।

questions.question: Does BFS from one node always visit the entire graph?
questions.answer: No. It only visits the connected component containing the starting node.

traps.statement: A visited array is optional in cyclic graphs.
traps.explanation: Without visited tracking, traversal may repeat nodes indefinitely.

topics.title: BREADTH-FIRST SEARCH (BFS)
topics.explanation: -Breadth First Search: BFS traverses a graph level-by-level using a FIFO Queue, guaranteeing the shortest path in unweighted graphs in O(V + E) time. Crucially, mark nodes as visited immediately when enqueuing—not dequeuing—to prevent duplicate entries and memory overflow.
topics.tldr: BFS Queue ব্যবহার করে এবং level by level explore করে।

codeSnippets.explanation: C++ BFS implementation using a queue.

questions.question: Does BFS always find the shortest path?
questions.answer: BFS finds the shortest path in terms of number of edges in an unweighted graph. For weighted graphs, use algorithms such as Dijkstra when appropriate.

traps.statement: BFS finds the shortest path in every graph.
traps.explanation: BFS finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs or when all edges have equal cost.

topics.title: DEPTH-FIRST SEARCH (DFS)
topics.explanation: -Depth-First Search: DFS explores a graph by traversing as deeply as possible along each branch before backtracking, utilizing a LIFO Stack or recursive call stack. Operating in O(V + E) time, it serves as the foundation for cycle detection, topological sorting, connected component discovery, and maze-solving algorithms.

codeSnippets.explanation: Iterative C++ DFS implementation using an explicit stack.

traps.statement: DFS always uses an explicit stack.
traps.explanation: DFS can use either an explicit stack or recursion.

topics.title: BFS VS DFS
topics.explanation: Difference: BFS uses a Queue to explore neighbors level-by-level, making it ideal for shortest path discovery in unweighted graphs. DFS uses a Stack (or recursion) to explore deeply down a single path before backtracking, making it the superior paradigm for connectivity, topological sorting, and cycle analysis.
topics.tldr: BFS আগে কাছের সব node দেখে, DFS আগে এক path যতদূর সম্ভব যায়।

comparisons.title: BFS vs DFS
rows: Good for shortest path in unweighted graph

questions.question: Which is better, BFS or DFS?
questions.answer: Neither is always better. The choice depends on the problem. Use BFS for level-based exploration and shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Use DFS for deep exploration, cycle detection, and topological problems.

sections.title: PART 3: HASHING
sections.description: Hash tables, collision handling, and container differences.

topics.title: HASHING FUNDAMENTALS
topics.explanation:
-Hashing: Hashing uses a hash function to map keys to table indices, giving average O(1) insert, search, and delete.
Collision: If distinct keys map to the same index (a collision), It is resolved via Separate Chaining (buckets hold linked lists/trees) or Open Addressing (probing next slots linearly or quadratically). Performance degrades to O(n) if excessive collisions overload buckets.
topics.tldr: Hashing average-এ খুব fast, কিন্তু collision বেশি হলে O(n) পর্যন্ত slow হতে পারে।

questions.question: Does hashing guarantee O(1) lookup?
questions.answer: No. O(1) is average-case performance. The worst case can be O(n).

traps.statement: Hash Tables always guarantee O(1).
traps.explanation: O(1) is average-case. Worst-case performance can be O(n).

topics.title: HASHMAP VS HASHSET
topics.explanation:
-HashMap: HashMap stores distinct Key-Value pairs, allowing fast lookups, updates, and indexing based on the key.
-Hashset: HashSet stores only individual unique elements without associated values, primarily used for fast O(1) membership testing and duplicate filtering.
topics.tldr: Map key-value রাখে, Set শুধু unique value রাখে।

questions.question: When should you use a HashSet instead of a HashMap?
questions.answer: Use a HashSet when you only need fast membership checking or duplicate detection and do not need associated values.

topics.title: C++ HASHMAP & HASHSET (unordered vs ordered)
topics.explanation: In C++, unordered_map and unordered_set are implemented via Hash Tables, offering average O(1) time complexity but no element ordering.

sections.title: PART 4: COMMON HASHING INTERVIEW PROBLEMS & CHEAT SHEETS
sections.description: Interview patterns, frequency counters, and revision cheat sheets.

topics.title: PROBLEM 1 — FREQUENCY COUNTER
topics.tldr: Count করতে হলে বেশিরভাগ সময় HashMap/Frequency Counter useful।

questions.question: Why is hashing better than nested loops for frequency counting?
questions.answer: Hashing can reduce the solution from O(n²) to O(n) average time by storing counts during a single traversal.

topics.title: PROBLEM 2 — TWO SUM
topics.tldr: Target থেকে current number বাদ দিয়ে complement Map-এ আছে কিনা check করো।

codeSnippets.explanation: JavaScript Two Sum solution using Map.

questions.question: Why check the complement before adding the current element?
questions.answer: This avoids incorrectly using the same element twice when the problem requires two different indices.

traps.statement: Why check the complement before adding the current element?
traps.explanation: This avoids incorrectly using the same element twice when the problem requires two different indices.

topics.title: PROBLEM 3 — DUPLICATE DETECTION
topics.tldr: আগে Set-এ আছে কিনা check করো, থাকলে duplicate পাওয়া গেছে।

questions.question: Why not use nested loops?
questions.answer: Nested loops take O(n²), while a HashSet solution takes O(n) average time.

topics.title: PROBLEM 4 — CHARACTER FREQUENCY
topics.tldr: String-এর character count দরকার হলে Map ব্যবহার করো।

questions.question: How can frequency counting help solve anagrams?
questions.answer: Two strings are anagrams if they contain the same characters with the same frequencies.

topics.title: HASHING PROBLEM-SOLVING CHEAT SHEET
topics.explanation:
A decision framework for selecting hashing strategies in technical interviews:
- Frequency / Counting → HashMap
- Duplicate Detection / Uniqueness → HashSet
- Instant Membership / Existence Check → HashSet
- Target Complement / Pair Search → HashMap
- Subarray Sum / Prefix Sum → HashMap (Prefix Sum → Index/Count)
- Unweighted Shortest Path → BFS
- Exhaustive Path Search / Backtracking → DFS
- Extreme Priority Tracking (Min/Max) → Heap / Priority Queue
- Direct Contiguous Index Access → Array

questions.question: When should you use an Adjacency Matrix vs Adjacency List?
questions.answer: Use an Adjacency Matrix when the graph is dense or when O(1) edge lookup is important. Use an Adjacency List when the graph is sparse because it uses O(V + E) space.

questions.question: Why do graph traversals use a visited array?
questions.answer: Graphs can contain cycles and multiple paths. A visited array prevents nodes from being processed repeatedly and avoids infinite loops.

questions.question: What is the main difference between BFS and DFS?
questions.answer: BFS uses a Queue and explores level by level. DFS uses a Stack or Recursion and explores one path deeply before backtracking.

questions.question: Array vs Linked List?
questions.answer: Arrays use contiguous memory and provide O(1) index access. Linked lists use nodes connected by pointers and provide efficient insertion or deletion when the position is already known.

questions.question: What is a Hash Collision?
questions.answer: A collision occurs when two different keys are mapped to the same hash table index. Common solutions include Separate Chaining and Open Addressing.

questions.question: Why can a Hash Table become O(n)?
questions.answer: A poor hash function or too many collisions can place many keys in the same bucket or probe sequence, making lookup linear.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Heap and a BST?
questions.answer: A Heap only guarantees the parent-child priority relationship. A BST guarantees ordering between the left subtree, node, and right subtree.

flashcards.question: What is the biggest advantage of an Array?
flashcards.answer: O(1) direct access using an index.

flashcards.question: When is Linked List insertion O(1)?
flashcards.answer: When the insertion position or node reference is already known.

flashcards.question: What principle does a Stack follow?
flashcards.answer: LIFO — Last In, First Out.

flashcards.question: What principle does a Queue follow?
flashcards.answer: FIFO — First In, First Out.

flashcards.question: Which data structure does BFS use?
flashcards.answer: Queue.

flashcards.question: Which data structure does DFS use?
flashcards.answer: Stack or Recursion.

What is a Hash Collision?
flashcards.answer: When two different keys map to the same table index.

flashcards.question: When does BFS find the shortest path?
flashcards.answer: In an unweighted graph, where each edge has equal cost.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between HashMap and HashSet?
flashcards.answer: HashMap stores key-value pairs. HashSet stores only unique values.

flashcards.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an array element by index?
What is the time complexity of searching for a value in an unsorted array?
flashcards.answer: O(n).

flashcards.question: Why are strings considered immutable in JavaScript?
flashcards.answer: Their characters cannot be changed directly after the string is created; modifying a string creates a new string.

flashcards.question: What is the amortized time complexity of vector push_back()?
flashcards.answer: O(1) amortized, although resizing can temporarily take O(n).

flashcards.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by position in a linked list?
flashcards.answer: O(n), because the list may need to be traversed from the beginning.

flashcards.question: What principle does a stack follow?
flashcards.answer: LIFO, or Last In, First Out.

flashcards.question: What principle does a queue follow?
flashcards.answer: FIFO, or First In, First Out.

flashcards.question: What is the main advantage of a circular queue?
flashcards.answer: It reuses empty spaces created by dequeue operations.

flashcards.question: What is the defining property of a binary tree?
flashcards.answer: Each node has at most two children: a left child and a right child.

flashcards.question: When does a BST provide average O(log n) search performance?
flashcards.answer: When the tree is reasonably balanced.

flashcards.question: Which tree traversal produces sorted output for a valid BST?
flashcards.answer: Inorder traversal.

flashcards.question: What does a heap guarantee about its elements?
flashcards.answer: It guarantees the heap property between each parent and its children, but it is not fully sorted.

flashcards.question: What is the space complexity of an adjacency matrix?
flashcards.answer: O(V²), where V is the number of vertices.

flashcards.question: When is an adjacency list preferred over an adjacency matrix?
flashcards.answer: For sparse graphs, because it uses O(V + E) space.

flashcards.question: What is the average lookup time of a hash table?
flashcards.answer: O(1) on average, although the worst case can be O(n) because of collisions.
